title: Recursive Models for Long-Horizon Reasoning
claim: Context management that stays in one sequence, even with summarization, keeps contexts growing; delegating subtasks to isolated recursive contexts avoids this.
layout: 3 stacked rows, left-to-right flow, nested dashed boxes in the final row
description: Three horizontally stacked diagrams, each with a bold caption underneath. Row (a) shows a standard autoregressive model. Input flows into a dashed box holding a long chain of gray Thoughts1…k blocks and ends in an Output block. Row (b) shows a single-context model with summarization. Gray Thoughts blocks are followed by green Summary blocks inside <sum> tags. A Context Manager arrow passes each summary into the next LLM Generator box, which runs as a chain of separate dashed boxes. Row (c) is the recursive model and takes the most space. A root dashed box holds Thoughts, <call> Subtask (blue) </call>, and Answer (red) blocks. Self-Call arrows drop to nested Depth 1 boxes, which contain still smaller Depth 2 recursion boxes. Return arrows carry the Answer back up. Yellow Input and Output blocks mark the ends. Color-coded tags (blue for call, red for return) carry the eye through the figure.
caption: Overview of different context management strategies.
abstract: Modern language models reason within bounded context, an inherent constraint that poses a fundamental barrier to long-horizon reasoning. We identify recursion as a core principle for overcoming this barrier, and propose recursive models as a minimal realization, where the model can recursively invoke itself to solve subtasks in isolated contexts. We prove that any computable problem admits a recursive decomposition of reasoning in which each subtask requires only exponentially smaller active context than standard autoregressive models; this strictly surpasses any context management approach confined to a single sequence, such as summarization. We further generalize our framework to modern agentic systems with arbitrary context processing and control flows, and prove that recursive models can achieve optimal power within this broader class. Experimentally, we test two settings: fine-tuning a pretrained base model for recursive SAT solving, and training a small model from scratch on Go traces generated by exact game-tree search. Both show improved long-horizon accuracy with small active contexts.
